Seg AX \(\perp\) ray YX and seg AZ \(\perp\) ray YZ, so AX and AZ are the distances of the point A from the two arms of \(\angle XYZ\). Point A lies on the bisector of \(\angle XYZ\), and every point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the arms of that angle. Therefore AZ = AX.
Hence AZ = 2 cm.

Seg PT \(\perp\) ray ST and seg PR \(\perp\) ray SR, so PT and PR are the distances of the point P from the two arms of \(\angle RST\). These distances are equal, since seg PR \(\cong\) seg PT.
A point in the interior of an angle that is equidistant from its arms lies on the bisector of that angle (the converse of the angle bisector theorem). So ray SP is the bisector of \(\angle RST\).
Therefore \(\angle RSP = \frac{1}{2}\angle RST = \frac{1}{2} \times 56^\circ\).
Hence \(\angle RSP = 28^\circ\), the reason being that P is equidistant from the arms of \(\angle RST\) and so lies on its bisector.

In a triangle, the greater side has the greater angle opposite to it.
Writing the sides in increasing order, \(PR = 8\) cm, \(PQ = 10\) cm, \(QR = 12\) cm.
The greatest side QR lies opposite \(\angle P\), so \(\angle P\) is the greatest angle. The smallest side PR lies opposite \(\angle Q\), so \(\angle Q\) is the smallest angle.
Hence the greatest angle is \(\angle P\) and the smallest angle is \(\angle Q\).

The angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\), so \(\angle N = 180^\circ - 80^\circ - 40^\circ = 60^\circ\).
Writing the angles in increasing order, \(\angle A = 40^\circ\), \(\angle N = 60^\circ\), \(\angle F = 80^\circ\).
In a triangle, the greater angle has the greater side opposite to it. The greatest angle \(\angle F\) lies opposite side AN, and the smallest angle \(\angle A\) lies opposite side FN.
Hence the greatest side is AN and the smallest side is FN, the reason being that the side opposite a greater angle is greater.

Let \(\triangle ABC\) be an equilateral triangle, so that AB = BC = CA.
In \(\triangle ABC\), seg AB \(\cong\) seg AC. By the isosceles triangle theorem the angles opposite congruent sides are congruent, and the angle opposite seg AB is \(\angle C\) while the angle opposite seg AC is \(\angle B\). Therefore \(\angle B \cong \angle C\).
Similarly seg BA \(\cong\) seg BC, and the angle opposite seg BA is \(\angle C\) while the angle opposite seg BC is \(\angle A\). Therefore \(\angle A \cong \angle C\).
Combining these, \(\angle A \cong \angle B \cong \angle C\), so the triangle is equiangular. (Since the three equal angles add to \(180^\circ\), each measures \(60^\circ\).)

Let the bisector of \(\angle BAC\) meet side BC at the point D, so that seg AD \(\perp\) side BC.
In \(\triangle ABD\) and \(\triangle ACD\):
\(\angle BAD \cong \angle CAD\) (seg AD bisects \(\angle BAC\)),
seg AD \(\cong\) seg AD (common side),
\(\angle ADB \cong \angle ADC\) (each measures \(90^\circ\), since seg AD \(\perp\) side BC).
The congruent sides lie between the two pairs of congruent angles, so by the ASA test \(\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACD\).
Therefore seg AB \(\cong\) seg AC (corresponding sides of congruent triangles), so two sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are congruent.
Hence \(\triangle ABC\) is an isosceles triangle.

In \(\triangle PQR\), seg PR \(\cong\) seg PQ, so by the isosceles triangle theorem the angles opposite them are congruent, that is \(\angle PQR = \angle PRQ\).
Since Q - R - S, ray RQ and ray RS are opposite rays, so \(\angle PRQ\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle PRS\) at R. An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of its remote interior angles, so \(\angle PRQ > \angle PSR\).
Combining, \(\angle PQR > \angle PSR\). Since Q - R - S, ray QS is the same ray as ray QR, so this says that in \(\triangle PQS\), \(\angle PQS > \angle PSQ\).
In a triangle the greater angle has the greater side opposite to it. In \(\triangle PQS\) the side opposite \(\angle PQS\) is seg PS and the side opposite \(\angle PSQ\) is seg PQ.
Therefore seg PS \(>\) seg PQ.

Seg AD and seg BE are altitudes, so \(\angle ADB = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle BEA = 90^\circ\). Hence \(\triangle ADB\) and \(\triangle BEA\) are right angled triangles whose hypotenuses are seg AB and seg BA respectively.
In \(\triangle ADB\) and \(\triangle BEA\):
\(\angle ADB \cong \angle BEA\) (each measures \(90^\circ\)),
hypotenuse AB \(\cong\) hypotenuse BA (the same segment),
seg DB \(\cong\) seg EA (given, BD = AE).
So by the hypotenuse-side test \(\triangle ADB \cong \triangle BEA\).
Therefore seg AD \(\cong\) seg BE (corresponding sides of congruent triangles).
